Public Comment–Opposition to
Hinckley Estates PUD
TO: Holladay City Planning Commission

FROM: Adjacent Property Owner – 4867 S. Floribunda Dr.


Summary Statement

We respectfully ask the Planning Commission to deny or delay approval of the proposed Hinckley
Estates PUD. Currently there are too many unknowns. Currently this proposal does not meet the
intent or standards of a Planned Unit Development under Holladay Code. It combines unrelated
properties across two unconnected streets, includes existing homes that will not change, and offers
no clear public benefit — only more flexibility for the applicant.

At its core, this appears to be a workaround to reconfigure property lines and to get smaller setbacks,
not a true cohesive development. It raises serious concerns around access, legal easement rights,
road maintenance, and inconsistent setbacks on our street. These issues directly affect adjacent
property owners and the long-term character of our neighborhood.

We want to be clear: we’re not opposed to new development. We believe it can happen within
existing zoning—and in a way that respects the shared identity of our neighborhood.

We only learned about this proposal 8 days before the public hearing. Many of us have rushed to
understand the details, but there’s only so much time. We plan to be in our home for the next 20+
years. Bottom line—we need more time, more clarity, and more conversation.



Hinkley Legacy & the Road Ahead

First, I want to acknowledge the Hinckley family’s legacy on this land—especially Jean Hinckley, who
has been its thoughtful steward for over 50+ years. Just last night, while working in our yard, we
visited with Jean. She shared how, in the 1930s, her father purchased this land from the original
homesteader. Later, on her seventh wedding anniversary, she planted the five towering pine trees
that now line the gravel road and driveways leading to our homes.

This is a special place. Jean has treated it like a personal preserve and has always graciously shared it
with her neighbors on Floribunda.

We live in what was once her brother’s home 4867 S. Floribunda Drive. At that time, the
Hinckleys owned all the surrounding land and placed the road where it made sense for their
family—not according to formal lot lines like you'd expect in a development today. In 1996, Jean
helped create a 0.5-acre lot for her brother by giving up a portion of her property. That’s also when
the Grant of Right-of-Way was recorded, granting access across 4891 S. Floribunda Drive, what
is now the Dellenbach property to Jean’s home, our home, and eventually the two vacant lots.

But the road, trees, and landscaping were never aligned to official boundaries. Many of the trees Jean
has lovingly maintained—and continues to maintain—are actually on a neighboring lot. The road
itself cuts diagonally across parcel lines. The Right-of-Way agreement requires benefiting parties to
share in road maintenance, but says nothing about how costs are divided or what happens if the road
is moved.

Any development forces a closer look at ROW implications, legal access, and property lines. A PUD
allows looser setbacks and greater flexibility—but before anything else moves forward, the road’s
status and responsibilities must be clearly understood and resolved.

Our hope is to better understand everyone’s goals and plans—while continuing the spirit of care that
Jean has upheld for decades. Let’s get it right, with clear agreements and a plan that honors the past,
respects the future, and protects everyone’s rights.



Not a True Planned Development

This proposal does not represent a cohesive or thoughtfully designed Planned Unit Development. It
combines two already-built, unrelated homes with two undeveloped lots solely to meet the minimum
threshold for a PUD. The existing homes will remain unchanged and are located on separate,
unconnected streets—one on Sleepy Hollow and the others on the private lane portion of Floribunda
Drive. These two areas are on different elevations and serve different street networks—they are not
naturally suited to a unified development.

At the neighborhood meeting, we asked, “Why a PUD?” The response was:​
“It’s the only way to flip the property lines to make the lot buildable.”

But that’s not accurate. Property line adjustments, lot consolidations, or flag lots are all regularly
used in Holladay for similar situations—no PUD required.

A PUD (Planned Unit Development) is not a zoning change—it’s a special overlay that allows more
flexible rules within existing zoning. The base zoning here remains R-1-10, but a PUD may allow
tighter setbacks, adjusted lot shapes, or clustered development—only if it offers a clear benefit to the
community.

That’s not what’s happening here:

    ●   No improved infrastructure
    ●   No integration between properties or streets
    ●   Two of the four homes already exist and will not change
    ●   No clear public benefit from including 2830 Sleepy Hollow—a home on a separate street that
        doesn’t need shared access

This doesn’t look like a planned development. It looks like a workaround to reconfigure lot lines and
relax development standards.
According to Holladay City Code §13.78.020:

       “A PUD is a privilege, not a right.”​
       “Applicants must justify to the Planning Commission why the project would be better
       for the community than a project developed under the underlying zoning.”

This application has not made that case. There’s no enhancement, no cohesion, and no integration.
It’s a patchwork—not a planned development.

Please review the map and visit the properties in person before coming to a decision.


No Access. No Easement.

This application prompted us to take a closer legal look at access rights across our property at 4867
S. Floribunda Drive. After reviewing records and consulting our attorney, we confirmed:

   ●    There is no recorded easement over our property.
   ●    Our 2017 survey and the 1996 survey both show the 30-foot right-of-way ending at the
        northern boundary of 4891 S. Floribunda Drive, which is the Dellenbach property.
   ●    The developer’s own drawings submitted to the city for this proposed PUD also show the
        right-of-way stopping at that same location.
   ●    There is nothing recorded on our title, and the county has no documentation showing
        otherwise.

We now have clarity: the 1996 “Grant of Right-of-Way” ends at the boundary between 4891 and 4867
S. Floribunda. The plat map confirms this termination point.

If anyone claims a prescriptive easement: there’s no legal basis. Our prior home owners and us were
either unaware or have always allowed our neighbors to use our road and driveway for access to the
existing home at 4880 S. Floribunda, and no other lots have used or required access across our
property. Under Utah law, a prescriptive easement requires open, notorious, adverse,
and continuous use for 20 years — all of these conditions must be met.

If access to new parcels is needed, it must be done properly—with consent, recorded easements,
and fair negotiation. That conversation has not happened.

I suggested to the Rennies to walk the property and view their survey flags, that hasn't happened yet
and we haven't noticed any physical survey markers. We’ve shared all our surveys and survey marker
photos from when we remodeled in 2017 in good faith to better understand things.

Until legal access is secured, the PUD shouldn’t move forward. Per Holladay Code §13.78.020, a
PUD “must not adversely affect adjacent properties.” Using or implying access without
permission does just that.

*[see separate file “Floribunda ROW comparison.pdf”
Right-of-Way Burden and Maintenance: Unresolved

Another major concern is the lack of clarity around road maintenance responsibilities tied to the
Grant of Right-of-Way — especially how it interacts with this proposed PUD.—especially in terms of
cost sharing, long-term upkeep, and governance.

The 1996 agreement identifies benefitted parcels: 4880 S. Floribunda (and its two associated lots)
and 4867 S. Floribunda. Those four parcels are required to share maintenance and repair costs for
the private lane. But now, the PUD includes four properties — on two different streets — and it’s
unclear how responsibilities will be divided.

   ●    Will properties on Sleepy Hollow, which don’t use the private lane, help maintain it?
   ●    When do the undeveloped lots begin contributing?
   ●    Is there a plan for snow removal, parking, or long-term road repairs?

Typically, a PUD includes an HOA or governing structure to manage shared infrastructure. But no
such plan has been presented. That introduces confusion, risk, and potential conflict.

Per Holladay Code §13.78.020, a PUD “must not adversely affect adjacent properties.”
This lack of transparency and shared governance does exactly that.

Until there’s a clear, coordinated agreement around access, maintenance, and cost sharing, the PUD
should not move forward.


Setbacks and Lot Widths Inconsistent with Floribunda

The proposed PUD would allow much smaller setbacks than currently exist on Floribunda. Our home
has setbacks of 15’, 36’, 15’, and 23’, and our neighbors’ lots are similar. The proposed PUD, directly
to our west, includes front setbacks as small as 20’—15 feet closer to the private lane than the 11
existing homes on Floribunda, all of which have 35’ or greater front setbacks. We’ve also been told
the PUD could allow setbacks as small as 4’, depending on future plans. This directly conflicts with
the 1996 recorded Covenants of Floribunda Heights, which require a 35’ minimum front setback.
While the private lane is technically outside the subdivision, those covenants were also signed by
families on the private lane—including Jean Hinckley and the Folsoms—reinforcing that this was a
shared neighborhood standard, not just a subdivision rule.

Plans and ownership can change, which is why it matters that the current proposal breaks from the
established pattern. Two new homes with significantly reduced setbacks will not match the standard
of the 11 that came before.

This is not consistent with Holladay Code §13.78.040, which requires that:

       “The proposed planned unit development shall be compatible with... existing
       development within the vicinity of the site.”

       Right now, the proposed PUD is not compatible. ​
       *[see separate file “Covenants - Floribunda Heights 4-26-1996 E#6341272.pdf”
Parking & Access

The current site plan shows driveway access across our property, but no recorded easement
exists to allow this. Without that legal access, we need to resolve where and how vehicles will
reach the proposed homes. Also parking is currently a problem. It will only get worse with
development. Now’s the time to discuss and plan.

Per Holladay Code §13.78.040, the PUD must address:

       “Parking area locations… which will adversely impact the reasonable use of adjacent
       property.”

This issue needs to be resolved before any approval moves forward.


Compliance is Already Possible

The proposed lots already meet the R-1-10 zoning requirements, which allow single-family homes on
lots of at least 10,000 square feet. Presently the undeveloped parcels in question are approximately
13,000 sq. ft. and 48,700 sq. ft. respectively — meaning the applicant has more than enough land to
configure both lots to meet size and frontage requirements.

Even if the orientation of the lots is flipped, or if access is shifted, these lots are still buildable under
standard zoning. Additional adjustments — like modest lot line shifts or even gifting square footage
between the two lots — could also be done through a standard lot line adjustment process, which
does not require PUD approval.

Per Holladay Code §13.78.020, PUD applicants:

       “must justify… why the project would be better for the community than a
       project developed as the underlying zoning would normally allow.”

In this case, the applicant has not demonstrated any public or community benefit — only a request
for flexibility in setbacks and layout. The project can proceed under standard zoning without a PUD.


Final Thoughts & Questions for the Committee

Floribunda has always felt like one street, even though it’s technically not. The homes are
single-family, well spaced, and follow consistent setbacks that give the street a standard. This
proposal doesn’t follow that pattern. It’s not a true planned development—it’s a workaround to move
lot lines, relax standards, and increase flexibility for the applicant.

We’re not opposed to new homes. We support responsible development that follows the base R-1-10
zoning—without the looser overlays of a PUD—and that respects legal access agreements, consistent
setbacks, and the shared identity of our street.
The current PUD proposal introduces too much uncertainty:​
– Access over private property with no easement
– No defined plan for road maintenance or shared costs
– Setbacks that conflict with the existing neighborhood
– No clear community benefit

If a PUD is a privilege—not a right—we ask:

   ●   Does a patchwork proposal like this align with your vision for Holladay neighborhoods?
   ●   Why pursue a PUD when the lots already meet zoning and the existing homes are staying
       as-is?
   ●   Why weren’t all neighbors on the private lane invited to participate? If this truly benefits the
       neighborhood, wouldn’t it make more sense to include everyone?
   ●   Why not take the time to present a clear plan that invites consensus from the other homes on
       the private lane—and leaves 2830 Sleepy Hollow Drive out of the PUD? If this really serves
       the neighborhood, let’s have that conversation together from the start—not as an
       afterthought.
   ●   Or, if the PUD isn’t the right path, we could honor the Hinckley legacy with a subdivision
       named in their honor, built under current R-1-10 zoning.

By design, a PUD allows greater flexibility than base zoning—reduced setbacks,
adjusted lot shapes, or clustering. While that flexibility can offer public benefit, it
can also be used to maximize land value by increasing development options. That’s
why the Holladay Code makes clear: a PUD is a privilege, not a right—and it
must not come at the expense of adjacent property owners or the character of the
neighborhood.

We urge you to delay or deny this proposal until there's a clearer, more inclusive, and legally sound
plan—one that reflects the standards, unity, and values of this neighborhood.

Christian & Amanda Hansen

From:               Tom Cloward
Sent:               Monday, May 5, 2025 12:34 PM
To:                 Carrie Marsh
Subject:            Residential Subdivision PUD-Hinckley Estates


[External Email - Use Caution]
Members of Holladay City Planning Commission:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the issue of a subdivision in the Hinckley Estates. We would like
to start by also thanking the Hinckley family for taking the time to introduce the possible future plans for
development at a neighborhood meeting.

Floribunda is a beautiful street with its large lots, mature trees, quite atmosphere and unique homes. Our
families have all been lucky enough to enjoy the beautiful, open, green space at the top of the Cul-de sac;
whether it has been our children playing in the snow, taking dogs for a walk or watching the deer.

It is not clear to us why there is really a need for the designation of a Planned Unit Development (PUD), how it
will affect our street or what it might mean for the future. Because the need for this change is not immediately
necessary, we would support delaying a decision until all parties have time to discuss matters and explore
alternative options. We would not like a PUD at the top of our street. We worry that this could lead to more
crowding, traffic and encroachment which is already becoming too prevalent in Holladay.

Thank you,
Tom and Carin Cloward

From:               Robert N
Sent:               Friday, May 2, 2025 6:15 PM
To:                 Carrie Marsh
Subject:            Public Hearing regarding "Hinckley Estates"


[External Email - Use Caution]

To: Carrie Marsh and the City of Holladay Planning Commission
From: Robert and Rachelle Nydegger - owner of 2870 Floribunda Drive
Summary Request: Please delay decision on the creation of the Hinckley Estates PUD until more
discussion and analysis can be conducted with residents on Floribunda Drive.
We are not trying to stop the development of 2 homes on the current vacant lots. We think 2
homes could ultimately be built within normal R1-10 zoning and be compatible with existing
homes and covenants on Floribunda.
When reading Holladay Utah Code 13.78.040 - we focus on - H.3 - Compatibility. This says "The
proposed planned unit development shall be compatible with the character of the site, adjacent
properties, and existing development within the vicinity of the site where the use will be located."
We think the single best measuring stick to being "compatible" is the Covenants signed (and
notarized) by Floribunda Heights residents on 4/26/1996, and ones that I understand are still on
county record. (It should be noted that when we knocked down the previous home on 2870
Floribunda and built our existing home in 2008, we did so with these covenants in mind).
These covenants state that homes shall be 35 feet from the front lot line. Why is it that a PUD,
instructed to be compatible with existing developments, will not honor the covenants of the
existing development? I believe the homes are sketched to be 20 feet from the front lot line. We
consider all properties bound by these covenants. This is the primary question we would like to
have time to discuss with all neighbors in Floribunda.
The proposers of the PUD (D and Christian Rennie) have said that they have no immediate
intention to build. They said they intend to move into the home of Jean Hinckley (4880 Floribunda
Drive), and after she passes away, build a new home on the adjacent lot. Being the case that there
is no immediate construction planned, we respectfully request a review period of a few months for
existing Floribunda residents to ascertain if we want to update the existing covenants or not. We
would warmly welcome D and Christian Rennie into those discussions too given their intentions to
ultimately build in the subdivision.
Please note, we are not against developing more homes, we just desire them to be compatible with
existing covenants and existing developments in the vicinity.
Sincerely, Rob and Shelly Nydegger
